title: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) in Diabetic Retinopathy & Retinal Detachment: A Comprehensive Guide
summary: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) is a cornerstone surgical procedure for managing complex vitreoretinal diseases, particularly sight-threatening complications of diabetic retinopathy and various forms of retinal detachment. This infographic explores the indications, principles, techniques, and considerations for PPV, providing a detailed, resident-level overview of this vital ophthalmic intervention.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) is a microscopic surgical procedure involving the removal of the vitreous gel from the posterior segment of the eye. This allows direct access to the retina and underlying structures for the treatment of various vitreoretinal pathologies. It is a critical intervention for complications of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) and complex Retinal Detachments (RD). Diabetic Retinopathy is a microvascular complication of diabetes, leading to retinal ischemia, neovascularization, and potentially severe vision loss. Retinal Detachment is the separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), a sight-threatening emergency.

sections.title: Risk Factors for DR & RD
content: **For Diabetic Retinopathy:** Duration of diabetes (most significant), poor glycemic control (HbA1c > 7%), hypertension, dyslipidemia, nephropathy, pregnancy.

**For Retinal Detachment:** Myopia (high axial length), previous cataract surgery (pseudophakia/aphakia), trauma, family history of RD, lattice degeneration, inflammation, Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR).

branches: Rhegmatogenous RD (RRD): Caused by a full-thickness retinal break (hole/tear), allowing vitreous fluid into subretinal space.
Tractional RD (TRD): Caused by vitreoretinal membranes pulling on the retina, lifting it off the RPE (common in PDR).
Exudative (Serous) RD: Caused by subretinal fluid accumulation from RPE/choroidal pathology (e.g., inflammation, tumor), without a break or traction.

sections.title: 6. Clinical Features & Symptoms (DR & RD)
content: **Diabetic Retinopathy:** Often asymptomatic in early stages. Symptoms include blurred vision, vision fluctuation, metamorphopsia (from macular edema), floaters (from vitreous hemorrhage), sudden painless vision loss (VH or TRD involving macula).

**Retinal Detachment:** Acute onset of 'flashes' (photopsia) and 'floaters' (new PVD/hemorrhage), progressive 'curtain' or 'shadow' in peripheral vision, decreased central vision (if macula involved), metamorphopsia, sensation of 'cobwebs'.

sections.title: 7. Ocular Examination Findings (DR & RD)
content: **Findings in DR:** Microaneurysms, dot/blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, IRMA, venous beading, neovascularization (NVD, NVE, NVI/NVA), pre-retinal hemorrhage, vitreous hemorrhage, fibrovascular membranes, macular edema (CME), tractional retinal detachment.

**Findings in RD:** Reduced visual acuity, afferent pupillary defect (if severe/macula-off), reduced IOP (may be normal or high in chronic cases), loss of red reflex, Shafer's sign (tobacco dust in anterior vitreous - pathognomonic for RRD), undulating/bullous detached retina, pigment demarcation lines (chronic RD), retinal breaks (holes, tears, dialysis), PVR (proliferative vitreoretinopathy - fixed folds, starfolds), specific for TRD: concave retinal surface, fixed folds, vitreous membranes, often no associated breaks in primary TRD.

sections.title: 9. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content:
**Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Examination**
   - Visual acuity, IOP measurement, Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (anterior segment, NVI/NVA).
   - Dilated fundus examination with indirect ophthalmoscopy and scleral depression (for full peripheral view, identifying breaks, extent of RD, traction).

**Step 2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**
   - High-resolution cross-sectional imaging of the retina.
   - Essential for diagnosing macular edema, ERM, VMT, subtle TRD, and assessing retinal attachment.

**Step 3: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA)**
   - Identifies areas of capillary non-perfusion, microaneurysms, neovascularization (leakage), macular edema, and IRMA.
   - Crucial for guiding PRP treatment.

**Step 4: B-scan Ultrasonography**
   - Indispensable when media opacities (dense VH, mature cataract) preclude direct visualization of the fundus.
   - Differentiates VH from RD, identifies choroidal detachment, IOFB, and assesses retinal configuration.

**Step 5: Systemic Workup (for DR patients)**
   - HbA1c, fasting blood glucose, blood pressure, renal function tests (serum creatinine, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio), lipid profile.
   - Optimizing systemic health is paramount for surgical success and long-term prognosis.

rows: Splitting of neurosensory layers (not full separation). Immobile, typically smooth and dome-shaped. Absence of Shafer's sign. May be bilateral. Absolute scotoma corresponding to the schisis.
Smooth, bullous, dark brown-orange elevations. Usually posterior to ora serrata. Associated with hypotony. 'Kissing choroidals' configuration. Does not undulate with eye movement.
Smooth, shifting subretinal fluid. No retinal breaks or traction. Associated with inflammatory conditions (e.g., Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada), tumors, severe hypertension, choroidal effusions.
Sudden vision loss/floaters. No 'curtain' unless settling. B-scan shows mobile echoes in vitreous, but retina attached. Red reflex may be dimmed/absent.
Usually stable, congenital or post-surgical. Retinal tissue is attached. OCT confirms folds without detachment.
Subretinal fluid/schisis in macula associated with congenital optic disc pit. Distinct fundus appearance of the optic nerve head.

sections.title: 11. Principles of Vitrectomy for Diabetic TRD
content:
**Step 1: Anesthesia & Trocar Placement**
   - Peribulbar or general anesthesia. 23G, 25G, or 27G trocar-cannula system placed through pars plana (3.5-4mm posterior to limbus), creating self-sealing sclerotomies.

**Step 2: Core Vitrectomy**
   - Removal of central clear vitreous with high-speed vitrectomy probe to gain access to posterior pole and release anterior traction.

**Step 3: Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) Induction (if absent)**
   - May use active aspiration (suction) with the vitrectomy probe or Tano-diamond dusted membrane scraper to induce PVD, if safely possible.

**Step 4: Membrane Segmentation & Delamination**
   - **Segmentation:** Cutting fibrotic membranes into smaller pieces to reduce tangential traction, often using micro-scissors or cutter.
   - **Delamination:** Peeling fibrovascular membranes off the retinal surface using intraocular forceps (e.g., Eckardt, serrated), picks, or MVR blades. Often requires bimanual technique (one hand for illumination, one for instruments) for counter-traction and stability. This is the most critical and challenging step.

**Step 5: Hemostasis**
   - Control bleeding from fibrovascular tissue using intraocular diathermy, increased infusion pressure, or temporary application of perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL).

**Step 6: Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) Peeling (if indicated)**
   - Peeling of residual ERM or internal limiting membrane (ILM) for macular holes or severe macular edema using diamond-dusted membrane peel forceps, often aided by vital dyes (e.g., brilliant blue G, indocyanine green).

**Step 7: Endolaser Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP)**
   - Application of 532nm green laser to the entire retina (excluding macula) to ablate ischemic areas and suppress neovascularization. Critical for preventing recurrence.

**Step 8: Fluid-Air Exchange (FAE) & Drainage of Subretinal Fluid (SRF)**
   - If a combined TRD/RRD or iatrogenic break occurs, FAE is performed to flatten the retina. SRF is drained through a retinal break (pre-existing or iatrogenic) using a soft-tipped cannula.

**Step 9: Vitreous Tamponade**
   - Injection of a vitreous substitute (air, gas, or silicone oil) to provide internal tamponade, support the retina, and facilitate fluid absorption/scarring. Choice depends on retinal pathology and surgeon preference.

**Step 10: Sclerotomy Closure**
    - Self-sealing sclerotomies with smaller gauges (23G, 25G, 27G) often require no sutures. 20G incisions always require suturing (e.g., 8-0 Vicryl).

sections.title: 12. Surgical Instruments & Techniques in PPV
content: **Vitrectomy Systems:** Modern high-speed systems (e.g., Alcon Constellation, Bausch & Lomb Stellaris Elite) with cutter speeds >10,000 cuts/minute and integrated laser/fluidics.
**Trocar-Cannula Systems:** 23-gauge (0.64mm), 25-gauge (0.50mm), 27-gauge (0.40mm) for micro-incisional vitrectomy (MIVS).
**Vitreous Cutters:** High-speed, dual-port cutters minimize vitreoretinal traction.
**Endo-illuminators:** Fiber optic light sources (standard, wide-angle, chandelier) for retinal visualization.
**Endo-laser Probes:** 532nm (green) diode lasers for PRP and focal photocoagulation.
**Membrane Forceps:** Delamination forceps (e.g., Eckardt, serrated), grasping forceps, micro-scissors for membrane dissection.
**Picks/Spatulas:** MVR blades, diamond-dusted scrapers, retinal picks for initiating membrane dissection or creating retinotomies.
**Visco-Dissection:** Use of viscoelastic agents (e.g., Healon, Viscoat) to hydro-dissect membranes off the retinal surface.
**Bimanual Surgery:** Using an instrument in each hand (e.g., light pipe in one, forceps in other) for optimal traction and dissection.

sections.title: 14. Complications of PPV & Prognosis
content: **Intra-operative Complications:** Iatrogenic retinal breaks (most common, 5-10%), choroidal hemorrhage, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, lens touch/damage, dropped nucleus, subretinal hemorrhage.
**Early Post-operative Complications:** Acute endophthalmitis (rare, <0.1%), vitreous hemorrhage (recurrent or new), hypotony/hypertony, choroidal detachment, fibrin reaction.

**Late Post-operative Complications:** Nuclear sclerotic cataract (universal with gas/oil), glaucoma (neovascular, steroid-induced, silicone oil-induced), redetachment (due to PVR, missed breaks), silicone oil emulsification/migration, corneal decompensation, epiretinal membrane formation, cystoid macular edema.

sections.title: Prognosis after PPV for TRD
content: **Retinal Reattachment Rates:** Generally high (80-90%) for TRDs with macula-on. Lower for macula-off or combined TRD/RRD with extensive PVR.

**Visual Outcomes:** Highly variable. Dependent on preoperative VA, duration of macula-off RD, extent of retinal damage, control of systemic diabetes, development of post-operative complications (especially cataract and glaucoma). Many patients achieve functional vision, but pre-existing damage may limit best-corrected vision.

sections.title: 15. Red Flags / Emergency Signs in DR/RD
content: **Acute onset of severe floaters and/or flashes:** Suggests acute PVD or new retinal break, potentially leading to RRD.
**Sudden, profound, painless vision loss:** May indicate dense vitreous hemorrhage (e.g., from PDR), macula-off retinal detachment, or central retinal artery occlusion.
**A 'curtain' or 'shadow' obscuring vision:** Classic symptom of progressive retinal detachment.
**Severe eye pain with vision loss in a diabetic patient:** Consider acute angle closure glaucoma (especially neovascular glaucoma in advanced DR) or endophthalmitis post-op.
**Persistent blurred vision or pain post-PPV:** Requires urgent evaluation for endophthalmitis, high IOP, or redetachment.

content.explanation: At least one of the following: 4 quadrants of severe intraretinal hemorrhages/microaneurysms; 2 quadrants of venous beading; 1 quadrant of prominent IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities). Crucial for determining progression to PDR.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Systemic Control is Key:** Tight glycemic control, blood pressure, and lipid management significantly impact DR progression and surgical outcomes.
**Pre-op Anti-VEGF:** Can reduce intraoperative bleeding and improve surgical planes in PDR/TRD by regressing fragile neovascularization.
**Always Examine Peripheral Retina:** After membrane peeling, always re-examine the peripheral retina thoroughly for iatrogenic breaks, especially near sclerotomy sites.
**Patient Positioning Post-op:** Crucial for gas tamponade (e.g., face down for macular hole, specific head position for superior breaks). Contraindicated for air travel with gas.
**Silicone Oil Removal:** Generally advised (typically 3-6 months post-op) due to potential long-term complications, unless a life-long tamponade is indicated.

**Pediatric Considerations:** While this infographic focuses on DR, PPV indications in children (e.g., ROP, FEVR, trauma) require specialized instruments, techniques, and anesthetic considerations due to smaller eyes and different vitreoretinal anatomy.

sections.title: 17. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
**Micro-Incisional Vitrectomy Systems (MIVS):** Transition from 20-gauge to 23G, 25G, and 27G has revolutionized PPV, offering smaller incisions, reduced conjunctival scarring, less post-op astigmatism, faster visual recovery, and typically sutureless closure. 

**Anti-VEGF Therapy:** DRCR.net studies (e.g., Protocol S, T) have solidified the role of anti-VEGF agents (e.g., Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, Bevacizumab) not only for diabetic macular edema but also as an adjuvant therapy in PDR, both pre-operatively to reduce active neovascularization and intra-operatively to minimize bleeding and facilitate membrane peeling. 

**3D Heads-Up Display Surgery:** Systems like Ngenuity (Alcon) and Artevo (Zeiss) project magnified, high-resolution 3D images onto a large screen, improving surgeon ergonomics, depth perception, and allowing the entire surgical team to view the operative field simultaneously. 

**Intraoperative OCT (iOCT):** Provides real-time, cross-sectional imaging during surgery, aiding in delicate membrane peeling, identifying subtle macular pathology, and ensuring complete retinal reattachment.
